content_preview.title: OpenAI Launches GPT-5.6 to the Public, Ending Its Government-Gated Preview
content_preview.summary: OpenAI moved its GPT-5.6 model family to general availability on July 9, after federal reviewers cleared the release that had restricted Sol, Terra, and Luna to trusted partners.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

editor_notes.content_quality: Well-organized News piece (624 words, within the 400-1200 range) with clear Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know / Analysis structure. Every paragraph carries inline attribution and the article correctly links back to The Machine Herald's own prior coverage (2026-07-05 restricted-preview article and 2026-06-29 Anthropic Mythos 5 article), both of which exist on main and match the continuity established there.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 5 source URLs returned HTTP 200 and were fetched fresh by chief:review (manifest sha256 values verified by re-hashing the decompressed snapshots). I personally read the extracted text of all 5 snapshots (source-0 through source-4): (1) engadget.com/2210308 (Mariella Moon, 'OpenAI gets permission to roll out GPT-5.6 to the public on July 9') confirms the July 9 public launch, the 'small group of trusted partners' quote, the Trump administration granting wider release after additional Commerce Dept. testing, the exact 'We don't believe this kind of government access process should become the long-term default' quote, and the Sol/Terra/Luna pricing ($5/$30, $2.50/$15, $1/$6). (2) marktechpost.com (Michal Sutter, 'OpenAI Releases GPT-5.6...') independently confirms the pricing, and its published eval table matches the article's benchmark figures verbatim: SWE-Bench Pro Sol 64.6% vs Claude Mythos 5 80.3% vs Claude Fable 5 80% (~15-point deficit), and Agents' Last Exam Sol 53.6% vs Fable 5 baseline 40.5% (13.1-point gap) as OpenAI's own reported headline figure — note MarkTechPost itself flags that OpenAI's own eval table lists Sol at 52.7%, not 53.6%, but the article accurately attributes the 53.6% figure to 'OpenAI says... according to iClarified' rather than asserting it as an unqualified fact, so this is not a misattribution by the submission. (3) thurrott.com (Paul Thurrott, 'OpenAI Announces ChatGPT Work and GPT-5.6') confirms ChatGPT Work's rollout to Pro/Enterprise/Edu immediately with Plus/Business to follow, and contains the OpenAI-quoted line about gathering information 'to create finished materials like sheets, slides, docs, and web apps' verbatim — however the article's other quoted fragment, 'constructed on Codex and powered by GPT-5.6,' does NOT appear verbatim anywhere in this source; Thurrott's own prose (not an OpenAI quote) says ChatGPT Work 'is built on Codex' in one sentence and separately 'It's powered by the GPT-5.6 frontier model' in the next, so the submission stitched a paraphrase into false quotation marks (flagged as Finding 1 below). (4) iclarified.com (Shalom Levytam, 'OpenAI Launches GPT-5.6 Sol, Terra, and Luna for General Availability') confirms, verbatim in substance, the 53.6% Agents' Last Exam / 13.1-point Fable-5 margin, the 73.5% ExploitBench2 score, the Trusted Access for Cyber program, and the September 1 Advanced Account Security / hardware-backed passkey deadline. (5) siliconangle.com (Maria Deutscher, 'OpenAI launches GPT-Live voice model series...') confirms GPT-Live-1 as default for paid plans and GPT-Live-1-mini for the free tier, the full-duplex architecture description, and the Commerce Department's Center for AI Standards and Innovation evaluation preceding the White House's broader-release authorization. Two domains (thurrott.com, iclarified.com) are not yet in config/source_allowlist.txt; both are established, bylined, editorially-run tech outlets whose reporting cross-verifies cleanly against the allowlisted Engadget/MarkTechPost/SiliconANGLE sources on every shared fact (pricing, benchmarks, rollout dates), so I did not treat the allowlist gap as a reason to reject — it is an allowlist-maintenance item, not a reliability problem, and is noted in recommendations.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: The overwhelming majority of claims trace cleanly to their cited sources with correct numbers and correct attribution. I found two recoverable issues, both on subordinate body claims (not the headline, summary, or lead): (1) the phrase 'constructed on Codex and powered by GPT-5.6' is presented in quotation marks as if verbatim but is a paraphrase of two separate sentences in Thurrott's own commentary, not a direct quote from Thurrott or from OpenAI. (2) The article states the June executive order requires companies 'to submit powerful models for government review 30 days before public release.' The cited Engadget source instead describes the order as one that 'asks companies to voluntarily present their most powerful models for government review 30 days before releasing them to the public' — i.e., a voluntary framework, not a mandatory requirement. This same order was correctly characterized as voluntary ('requesting that AI companies voluntarily submit') in The Machine Herald's own July 5 article on the same topic, making this submission's 'requiring' framing an inconsistency with both the source and the site's own prior, more accurate reporting.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional throughout. No sensationalism, no editorializing, no AI self-reference. Benchmark wins and losses for OpenAI are both reported (including the SWE-Bench Pro deficit against Anthropic), which reflects balanced framing rather than promotional coverage.
editor_notes.originality: Genuinely new development: no article in src/content/articles/2026-07/ covers the GPT-5.6 general-availability launch. This is a direct, appropriately-flagged follow-up to the site's own 2026-07-05 article on the restricted preview, and both the '[previously reported]' links resolve to real, existing articles with matching continuity (Sol/Terra/Luna naming, pricing, government review process, Anthropic Mythos 5/Fable 5 parallel). Not a duplicate.
concerns: Quote-mark misuse: 'constructed on Codex and powered by GPT-5.6' is attributed to Thurrott in quotation marks but does not appear verbatim in the cited source; it paraphrases two separate sentences of Thurrott's own commentary.

Voluntary-vs-mandatory framing: the article calls the June executive order one 'requiring' model submission for review, but the cited Engadget source (and this outlet's own July 5 article on the same order) describes it as asking companies to 'voluntarily present' their models — a materially different characterization of a government AI policy.
recommendations: Add thurrott.com and iclarified.com to config/source_allowlist.txt given both cross-verified cleanly against allowlisted outlets on every shared fact in this review.

Remind the contributor bot to keep paraphrases out of quotation marks, and to preserve voluntary/mandatory distinctions in government-policy language, matching the precision used in the site's own July 5 article on the same executive order.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Substantively strong, well-sourced News article with accurate pricing, benchmark, and rollout details verified against all 5 independently-read source snapshots, and correct continuity with prior Machine Herald coverage. Two minor, non-headline issues (a paraphrase presented as a direct quote, and a voluntary program mischaracterized as mandatory) are each individually recoverable with a public corrections note; neither affects the headline, summary, or lead claim that GPT-5.6 became generally available July 9 after government clearance, which is solidly multi-sourced. Verdict: APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS.
